contrast: American spelling is *drafty*; British English writes *draughty*.

senses.gloss: Letting in currents of cold air.
examples: The old farmhouse was *drafty* in the winter.
We put plastic over the *drafty* windows.
The upstairs bedroom is even *draftier* than the living room.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *I feel drained*
contrast: *drained* is how you feel; *draining* is what makes you feel that way: *The trip was draining, and I was drained*.

senses.gloss: Very tired, with no energy or emotion left.
examples: After the funeral, everyone felt completely *drained*.
She came home from her shift looking *drained*.
I was more *drained* by the meeting than by the eight-hour drive.

senses.gloss: Making you feel very tired and without energy.
examples: Caring for a sick parent is emotionally *draining*.
It was a long, *draining* week at work.
Online classes were more *draining* than I expected.

senses.gloss: Extreme and sudden, with a strong effect.
examples: The company took *drastic* steps to cut costs.
Don't do anything *drastic* until we talk.
The change in her appearance was more *drastic* than I'd imagined.

position: both — mostly after *look*: *She looked pale and drawn*
contrast: In *I've always been drawn to the ocean* (attracted to) and *with the curtains drawn* (closed), *drawn* is the verb *draw* in the passive.

senses.gloss: Looking thin, pale and tired because of worry, illness or pain.
examples: His face was *drawn* after three nights in the hospital.
She looked pale and *drawn* at the trial.
He seemed more *drawn* every time I visited.

position: both — often *long, drawn-out*; after a verb usually *drawn out*: *The process was drawn out*

senses.gloss: Lasting longer than necessary or than you want.
examples: The divorce was a long, *drawn-out* process.
Nobody wanted another *drawn-out* legal battle.
This year's budget talks were even more *drawn-out* than last year's.

position: attributive only — usually *the dreaded*: *the dreaded phone call*

senses.gloss: Feared or strongly disliked; often used humorously about something unpleasant but ordinary.
examples: Then came the *dreaded* question: "So, when are you getting married?"
My laptop showed the *dreaded* blue screen.
For many students, the SAT is the *most dreaded* test of high school.

senses.gloss: Very bad or very unpleasant.
examples: The food at the hotel was *dreadful*.
We heard about the *dreadful* accident on the news.
It was the *most dreadful* movie I've ever sat through.

senses.gloss: Feeling ill, or feeling very sorry or guilty about something.
examples: I feel *dreadful* about forgetting your birthday.
She had the flu and looked *dreadful*.

senses.gloss: Strange, unreal or beautiful, as if happening in a dream.
examples: The fog gave the valley a *dreamlike* quality.
The whole wedding day felt *dreamlike*.
His later paintings became more *dreamlike* and abstract.

senses.gloss: Thinking about pleasant things and not paying attention to what is happening.
examples: She had a *dreamy* look on her face.
He was a quiet, *dreamy* kid who loved to read.

senses.gloss: Soft, gentle and pleasant, like something in a dream.
examples: The band plays slow, *dreamy* pop songs.
This cake is even *dreamier* with whipped cream.

senses.gloss: Informal: very attractive.
examples: Her new boyfriend is so *dreamy*.
The actor was voted the *dreamiest* guy in Hollywood.

senses.gloss: Dull, gray and depressing.
examples: It was a cold, *dreary* day in February.
The office was *dreary*, with no windows at all.
His second novel is even *drearier* than his first.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *We got drenched*
takes: *in* or *with* + noun: *drenched in sweat*, *drenched with rain*

senses.gloss: Completely wet.
examples: We got caught in the storm and came home *drenched*.
His shirt was *drenched* in sweat.
She pulled off her *drenched* socks.

position: both — alone after a verb: *get dressed*; before a noun with an adverb: *a well-dressed man*
takes: *in* + clothes or color: *dressed in black*; *as* + character: *dressed as a pirate*; *for* + occasion: *dressed for work*
contrast: Russian says *одеваться*, but English says *get dressed*, not *dress myself* in everyday speech. *dressed up* means wearing formal or special clothes: *Why are you all dressed up?*

senses.gloss: Wearing clothes, not naked or in pajamas.
examples: Hurry up and get *dressed* — the bus is coming.
I'm not *dressed* yet, so don't open the door.
He was fully *dressed* by six in the morning.

senses.gloss: Wearing a particular kind or style of clothes.
examples: She was *dressed* in a long blue coat.
The kids were *dressed* as superheroes for Halloween.
He's always well *dressed* for meetings.

senses.gloss: Of clothes or an event: formal and elegant, not casual.
examples: Is the party *dressy*, or can I wear jeans?
She bought a *dressy* black jacket for the wedding.
You'll need something *dressier* than that sweater.

position: attributive only — after a verb English usually says *dry*: *The paint is dry*

senses.gloss: With the water removed so that it keeps for a long time.
examples: Add a cup of *dried* cranberries to the salad.
The recipe calls for *dried* beans, not canned ones.
She hung bunches of *dried* flowers in the kitchen.

position: both — after a verb usually *dried up*: *The creek is dried up*

senses.gloss: With all the water gone; no longer wet, fresh or full of life.
examples: We walked along a *dried-up* riverbed.
The flowers on the table were brown and *dried-up*.
All that was left of the lake was a *dried-up* patch of mud.

senses.gloss: Clean and safe enough to drink.
examples: Is the tap water *drinkable* here?
The filter makes stream water *drinkable*.

senses.gloss: Of wine, beer or coffee: pleasant and easy to drink.
examples: It's a cheap but very *drinkable* red wine.
The coffee got more *drinkable* after I added milk.

form: past participle of *drive*; also a suffix: *data-driven*, *market-driven*

senses.gloss: Extremely determined to succeed and working very hard.
examples: She's a *driven* young lawyer who works seventy hours a week.
Even as a teenager, he was incredibly *driven*.
My sister was always *more driven* than I was.

contrast: In *driving lessons* and *a driving test*, *driving* is a noun (the activity of driving a car) used as a modifier, not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Of rain or snow: falling very hard and blown by the wind.
examples: We changed the tire in *driving* rain.
The hikers turned back in the *driving* snow.

senses.gloss: Having a strong influence that makes something happen.
examples: She was the *driving* force behind the project.
Fear of losing customers was the *driving* factor in the decision.

senses.gloss: With light, fine rain falling.
examples: It was a gray, *drizzly* morning in Seattle.
The weather stayed *drizzly* all weekend.
The coast is usually more *drizzly* than the valley.

contrast: *droll* is quiet, dry, clever humor — not loud or silly. It is a bookish word; everyday speech says *funny* or *dry*.

senses.gloss: Funny in a quiet, clever or unusual way.
examples: He has a *droll* sense of humor.
"Well, that went well," she said in a *droll* voice.
Her essays are more *droll* than laugh-out-loud funny.

senses.gloss: Hanging down, often because of being weak or tired.
examples: The basset hound has long, *droopy* ears.
My plants get *droopy* if I forget to water them.
His eyelids got *droopier* as the lecture went on.

senses.gloss: Tired and almost asleep.
examples: This medicine may make you *drowsy*.
Don't drive if you feel *drowsy*.
The warm room made everyone *drowsier* after lunch.

senses.gloss: Where illegal drugs are not used or allowed.
examples: The sign said "*Drug-Free* School Zone."
He has been *drug-free* for five years.

senses.gloss: Done without using medicine.
examples: She wanted a *drug-free* birth.
Physical therapy is a *drug-free* way to manage back pain.

senses.gloss: Sleepy or confused because of a drug.
examples: After the surgery, he was still *drugged* and couldn't talk.
She woke up feeling *drugged* and heavy.

senses.gloss: Of food or drink: with a drug secretly added.
examples: Police believe the victim was given a *drugged* drink.
The guard fell asleep after eating the *drugged* sandwich.

takes: *on* + drink: *drunk on cheap wine*; *with* or *on* + feeling: *drunk with power*
contrast: *drunken* also means 'drunk' but goes only before a noun and often describes behavior: *a drunken fight*. *a drunk* is a noun, 'a person who is often drunk'. The verb forms are *drink, drank, drunk*: *I have drunk*, not *I have drank*.

senses.gloss: Having had so much alcohol that you cannot think or act normally.
examples: He got *drunk* at his brother's wedding.
A *drunk* driver ran the red light.
She was *drunker* than anyone else at the party.

senses.gloss: So excited by a feeling that you do not act sensibly.
examples: The new manager was *drunk* with power.
They were *drunk* on their early success.

contrast: Sounds exactly like *duel*, 'a fight between two people'.

senses.gloss: Having two parts, uses or roles.
examples: She holds *dual* citizenship in the US and Canada.
The room serves a *dual* purpose as an office and a guest room.
The car has *dual* airbags in the front.

takes: *about* or *of* + noun, when it means 'doubtful': *dubious about the plan*

senses.gloss: Probably not honest, true, good or legal.
examples: The website makes some *dubious* claims about weight loss.
He made his money in some *dubious* business deals.
They won the *dubious* honor of being the worst team in the league.

senses.gloss: Not sure that something is good or true.
examples: I was *dubious* about his plan at first.
My parents were even *more dubious* than I was.

senses.gloss: Boring and not interesting.
examples: The lecture was long and *dull*.
Life in a small town can be *dull*.
This is the *dullest* book I've ever read.

senses.gloss: Not bright or shiny; of weather, gray and cloudy.
examples: The paint had faded to a *dull* green.
It was a *dull*, overcast afternoon.

senses.gloss: Of a blade: not sharp.
examples: Be careful — a *dull* knife slips more easily.
These scissors are getting *duller* every week.

senses.gloss: Of a pain or sound: not strong or clear.
examples: I have a *dull* ache in my lower back.
We heard a *dull* thud from upstairs.

contrast: The *b* is silent. In everyday American English *dumb* means 'stupid'. The old meaning 'unable to speak' is offensive about people; say *nonspeaking* or *unable to speak*. It survives in *struck dumb*.

senses.gloss: Informal: stupid.
examples: That was a really *dumb* mistake.
Don't ask *dumb* questions.
It's the *dumbest* movie I've seen all year.

senses.gloss: For a short time unable to speak because of shock or surprise.
examples: We were struck *dumb* by the news.
She stood there *dumb* with amazement.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *I was dumbfounded*

senses.gloss: So surprised that you cannot speak.
examples: I was completely *dumbfounded* by her answer.
He stared at the bill with a *dumbfounded* expression.
The fans sat in *dumbfounded* silence after the loss.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *She was dumbstruck*

senses.gloss: So shocked or amazed that you cannot speak.
examples: The audience was *dumbstruck* by the ending.
He stood *dumbstruck* in the doorway.
She gave me a *dumbstruck* look.

senses.gloss: Of a person or thing: short and fat; not a kind word.
examples: The character was a *dumpy* little man in a brown suit.
She felt *dumpy* in the oversized sweater.

senses.gloss: Informal, of a place: dirty, old and in bad condition.
examples: We stayed in a *dumpy* motel off the highway.
Their first apartment was even *dumpier* than this one.

contrast: The adjective and noun end in /kət/; the verb *to duplicate* ends in /keɪt/: *a DOO-pli-kuht key*, but *don't DOO-pli-kayt the work*.

senses.gloss: Exactly the same as something else; made as a copy.
examples: I had a *duplicate* key made at the hardware store.
The system found two *duplicate* files.
Please don't send *duplicate* payments.

senses.gloss: Dishonest; saying one thing and secretly doing another.
examples: The senator was accused of being *duplicitous*.
It was a *duplicitous* scheme to cheat investors.
The villain in the second season is even more *duplicitous*.

senses.gloss: Staying in good condition or lasting for a long time.
examples: These boots are made of *durable* leather.
Plastic plates are *more durable* than glass ones.
Both sides hoped for a *durable* peace.

senses.gloss: In economics, of goods: expected to be used for several years, like cars and refrigerators.
examples: Orders for *durable* goods fell last month.
Washing machines and furniture count as *durable* goods.

senses.gloss: Covered with or full of dust.
examples: We found old photos in a *dusty* box in the attic.
The roads get *dusty* in August.
The back shelves were the *dustiest* in the store.

senses.gloss: Of a color: soft and slightly gray.
examples: The bridesmaids wore *dusty* pink.
The walls are painted a *dusty* blue.

senses.gloss: Doing what you should do or what others expect, often without enthusiasm.
examples: She was a *dutiful* daughter who visited her mother every Sunday.
The audience gave *dutiful* applause.
He was more *dutiful* than his brothers about calling home.

position: predicative only — *I feel duty-bound to tell you*

senses.gloss: Having to do something because it is your duty.
examples: I felt *duty-bound* to report the mistake.
Doctors are *duty-bound* to protect patient privacy.
As his lawyer, she was *duty-bound* to keep the secret.

contrast: It is also an adverb: *You can buy perfume duty-free at the airport*.

senses.gloss: Sold without government import taxes.
examples: We picked up some chocolate at the *duty-free* shop.
Is this bottle of wine *duty-free*?
You're allowed one liter of *duty-free* alcohol.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the verb *dwindle*: *Supplies are dwindling*

senses.gloss: Becoming gradually smaller in number or amount.
examples: The town has a *dwindling* population.
Rescuers worked with *dwindling* hope of finding survivors.
The team is running on *dwindling* funds.

contrast: *dyed* (colored with dye) and *died* (from *die*) sound exactly the same.

senses.gloss: Colored with a dye.
examples: She has *dyed* purple hair.
Is your hair *dyed*, or is that your natural color?
The shirts were *dyed* with natural plant colors.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the verb *die*: *He is dying*
contrast: Informal *I'm dying to see it* (I want it very much) and *I'm dying for a coffee* are verb uses. Don't confuse with *dyeing* (coloring with dye).

senses.gloss: About to die.
examples: The nurse sat with the *dying* man all night.
We couldn't save the *dying* tree in the yard.

senses.gloss: Disappearing or coming to an end.
examples: Hand-sewing shoes is a *dying* art.
Honest politicians are a *dying* breed.

senses.gloss: Happening at the moment of death or in the last part of something.
examples: It was her *dying* wish to see the ocean again.
They scored in the *dying* seconds of the game.

contrast: *dynamics* and *a dynamic* are nouns: *family dynamics*, *the dynamic between them*.

senses.gloss: Full of energy, new ideas and enthusiasm.
examples: We're looking for a *dynamic* leader.
She's one of the *most dynamic* speakers I've heard.

senses.gloss: Always changing and developing.
examples: The job market is *dynamic* and hard to predict.
Language is a *dynamic* system, not a fixed set of rules.

senses.gloss: Relating to a family that holds power for many generations.
examples: The kingdom was torn apart by *dynastic* wars.
Some voters worry about *dynastic* politics in the party.
The *dynastic* marriage joined two royal houses.

senses.gloss: Of a family, group or relationship: not working in a normal, healthy way.
examples: He grew up in a *dysfunctional* family.
Congress has become more *dysfunctional* than ever.
The office culture was completely *dysfunctional*.

senses.gloss: Of a body part or system: not working properly.
examples: Tests showed a *dysfunctional* thyroid gland.
The old heating system is basically *dysfunctional*.

senses.gloss: Having dyslexia, a condition that makes reading and spelling difficult.
examples: My son is *dyslexic*, so he gets extra time on tests.
The school offers support for *dyslexic* students.
She didn't find out she was *dyslexic* until college.

senses.gloss: Describing an imagined future society where life is frightening and people are controlled or suffer.
examples: *The Hunger Games* is a *dystopian* novel.
The empty city streets felt almost *dystopian*.
Each season of the show gets more *dystopian*.

senses.gloss: Very good at seeing or noticing small details.
examples: An *eagle-eyed* reader spotted the typo on page one.
The goalie was *eagle-eyed* all game.
The *most eagle-eyed* fans noticed the hidden clue in the trailer.

contrast: *in earnest* is a phrase: *The work began in earnest* (seriously, fully); *Are you in earnest?* (Do you really mean it?).

senses.gloss: Very serious and sincere, sometimes too serious.
examples: He's an *earnest* young man who wants to help.
They had a long, *earnest* conversation about the future.
Her second speech was *more earnest* and less funny.

senses.gloss: Made of earth or baked clay.
examples: The old cabin had an *earthen* floor.
Engineers inspected the *earthen* dam after the flood.
Water was kept cool in large *earthen* jars.

senses.gloss: Relating to life in this world, not to heaven or the spirit.
examples: He gave away all his *earthly* possessions.
Their *earthly* life was hard, but their faith was strong.

senses.gloss: After *no*, *any* or *what*: at all, possible.
senses.ru: какой бы то ни было, никакой
examples: There's no *earthly* reason to wake up at five.
What *earthly* use is a phone without a battery?

senses.gloss: Tasting, smelling or looking like soil.
examples: Mushrooms have an *earthy* flavor.
The room was decorated in warm, *earthy* colors.
This coffee is *earthier* than the Colombian one.

senses.gloss: Direct and natural, and not shy about the body or sex.
examples: She has an *earthy* sense of humor.
His grandmother was a warm, *earthy* woman who laughed a lot.

contrast: In *drive east* it is an adverb, and in *the East* a noun. *east* is mostly for fixed names and parts: *the East Coast*, *the east side*; *eastern* is the general word: *eastern Europe*, *eastern states*.

senses.gloss: In, on or facing the east.
examples: They live on the *east* side of town.
Take the *east* exit from the parking garage.
We moved to the *East* Coast last year.

senses.gloss: Of wind: blowing from the east.
examples: A cold *east* wind blew all day.
The *east* winds brought rain from the ocean.

senses.gloss: Of or from eastern Africa, such as Kenya, Tanzania, Ethiopia or Uganda.
examples: *East African* runners dominate long-distance races.
The restaurant serves *East African* food.
Swahili is spoken in many *East African* countries.

contrast: Historical: the German Democratic Republic existed from 1949 to 1990. For the region today, say *eastern German* or *in eastern Germany*.

senses.gloss: Of or from the former German Democratic Republic.
examples: His parents escaped from *East German* territory in 1961.
*East German* athletes won many Olympic medals.
The car she drove was *East German*.

senses.gloss: Traveling or leading toward the east.
examples: There's a crash in the *eastbound* lanes of I-90.
The *eastbound* train leaves at 7:15.
Is this platform *eastbound* or westbound?

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an easterly wind*
comparison: not gradable — but *most easterly* means 'farthest east'
contrast: An *easterly* wind blows *from* the east, but an *easterly* direction is *toward* the east.

senses.gloss: Toward or in the east.
examples: The ship sailed in an *easterly* direction.
Maine is the *most easterly* state in the country.

senses.gloss: Of wind: blowing from the east.
examples: Strong *easterly* winds kept the boats in the harbor.
The forecast calls for light *easterly* breezes.

contrast: In American English the Russian Church is usually called *Russian Orthodox*; *Eastern Orthodox* names the whole family of Orthodox churches. *orthodox* with a small *o* means 'traditional, accepted': *orthodox methods*.

senses.gloss: Of the Orthodox Christian churches of Eastern Europe, Greece and the Middle East.
examples: Most of her family is *Eastern Orthodox*.
*Eastern Orthodox* Christians often celebrate Easter on a different date.
They were married in an *Eastern Orthodox* church in Chicago.

comparison: not gradable — it is already a superlative

senses.gloss: Farthest to the east.
examples: Lubec, Maine, is the *easternmost* town in the US.
We visited the *easternmost* point of the island.
The *easternmost* part of the state is mostly farmland.

contrast: After a verb it is an adverb: *The storm moved eastward*. *eastwards* with an *s* is more British.

senses.gloss: Moving or facing toward the east.
examples: The storm continued its *eastward* path.
Our *eastward* flight took only four hours.
The house has an *eastward* view of the mountains.

form: compound — *easy* + *going*; one word in American spelling

senses.gloss: Relaxed and calm, not easily upset or worried.
examples: My new roommate is really *easygoing*.
He has an *easygoing* attitude about money.
She's much *more easygoing* than her sister.

senses.gloss: Very cheerful, excited and full of energy.
examples: The coach was in an *ebullient* mood after the win.
She's an *ebullient* host who makes everyone feel welcome.
He was even *more ebullient* than usual at the reunion.

contrast: *an eccentric* is also a noun: *He's a lovable eccentric*.

senses.gloss: Behaving or looking strange and unusual, often in a harmless or amusing way.
examples: My *eccentric* uncle keeps goats in his backyard.
Her fashion sense is a little *eccentric*.
He got *more eccentric* as he got older.

senses.gloss: Made up of many different styles, types or ideas.
examples: He has *eclectic* taste in music, from jazz to heavy metal.
The café is decorated in an *eclectic* mix of styles.
This year's lineup is *more eclectic* than ever.

contrast: False friend: Russian *экологичный* or *экологически чистый* is *eco-friendly*, *green* or *environmentally friendly* in English: *eco-friendly packaging*, not *ecological packaging*. *ecological* means 'relating to nature and the environment': *an ecological disaster*.

senses.gloss: Relating to the relationships between living things and their environment.
examples: The oil spill was an *ecological* disaster.
Scientists are studying the *ecological* impact of the new dam.
Wetlands have enormous *ecological* value.

senses.gloss: Of or from Ecuador, its people or its culture.
examples: We tried *Ecuadorian* ceviche in Queens.
Her father is *Ecuadorian* and her mother is Peruvian.
The *Ecuadorian* coast is famous for its bananas and shrimp.

position: both — the religious sense mostly before a noun: *an ecumenical service*
comparison: not gradable — but *more ecumenical* in the 'broad' sense

senses.gloss: Bringing together different Christian churches or different religions.
examples: The town held an *ecumenical* prayer service after the tragedy.
Leaders from several churches joined the *ecumenical* council.

senses.gloss: Including or accepting many different kinds of things.
examples: The festival takes an *ecumenical* approach to music.
Her reading habits are wonderfully *ecumenical*.

senses.gloss: Nervous, tense and easily annoyed.
examples: Everyone was *edgy* while we waited for the results.
Too much coffee makes me *edgy*.

senses.gloss: Daring, modern and a little shocking.
examples: The comedian is known for his *edgy* jokes.
The band's new album is *edgier* than their last one.

comparison: not gradable — but *barely edible*, *more edible* when it means 'good enough to eat'
contrast: *edibles* is a plural noun, in American English often 'food containing cannabis'.

senses.gloss: Safe to eat.
examples: Not all wild mushrooms are *edible*.
The flowers on the cake are *edible*.
We learned to find *edible* plants in the woods.

senses.gloss: Good enough to eat, though not very good.
examples: The cafeteria food was barely *edible*.
With some salt, the soup was at least *edible*.

contrast: *an editorial* is a noun: an article that gives a newspaper's opinion.

senses.gloss: Relating to editing or to the people who prepare a book, newspaper or magazine.
examples: She joined the magazine's *editorial* staff.
The paper insists on its *editorial* independence.

senses.gloss: Giving an opinion rather than just reporting facts.
examples: The *editorial* page supported the mayor.
He draws *editorial* cartoons for a local paper.

senses.gloss: Having had a good education and knowing a lot.
examples: She's an *educated* woman who speaks three languages.
Voters in the suburbs tend to be *more educated*.
He was *educated* at a small college in Ohio.

senses.gloss: Of a guess or decision: based on some knowledge, so likely to be right.
examples: I don't know the exact number, but I can make an *educated* guess.
Read the reviews so you can make an *educated* choice.

position: both — the 'relating to education' sense only before a noun: *the educational system*
comparison: more/most — *more educational*, *most educational*, in the 'teaches you something' sense

senses.gloss: Relating to education and schools.
examples: The *educational* system needs more funding.
He works for an *educational* nonprofit.

senses.gloss: Teaching you something useful or interesting.
examples: The trip to the museum was really *educational*.
We try to buy *educational* toys for the kids.
The documentary was *more educational* than the textbook.

senses.gloss: From the time of King Edward VII of Britain, 1901 to 1910, or in its style.
examples: They restored a beautiful *Edwardian* house.
The movie is set in *Edwardian* England.
The costumes in the play were *Edwardian*.

senses.gloss: Strange and frightening in a mysterious way.
examples: An *eerie* silence fell over the empty school.
It was *eerie* how much he looked like his late father.
The abandoned mall is *eerier* at night.

contrast: Used about men and usually disapproving or offensive. It is not a neutral word for *feminine*.

senses.gloss: Of a man: looking or behaving in a way thought to be typical of women.
examples: He was bullied at school for being *effeminate*.
Critics called the singer's style *effeminate*.
In the remake, the character is less *effeminate* and more serious.

senses.gloss: Of a person: lively, cheerful and full of energy.
examples: She has an *effervescent* personality.
The *most effervescent* guest at the party was my grandmother.

senses.gloss: Of a liquid: producing small bubbles of gas.
examples: Drop the *effervescent* tablet into a glass of water.
The wine is light and slightly *effervescent*.

contrast: A disapproving, bookish word; in American political talk it often mocks educated elites: *effete snobs*.

senses.gloss: Weak, too refined and lacking energy or strength.
examples: The novel mocks the *effete* aristocrats of old Europe.
He dismissed his critics as *effete* intellectuals.
The new version sounds *more effete* than the original.

senses.gloss: Done so well that it seems to need no effort.
examples: She made the difficult dance look *effortless*.
He has an *effortless* style of writing.
Her piano playing grew *more effortless* every year.

senses.gloss: Showing strong feelings of praise, thanks or welcome, sometimes too much.
examples: The reviews of the play were *effusive*.
He gave me an *effusive* welcome at the door.
She was *more effusive* in her thanks than I expected.

senses.gloss: Believing that all people are equal and should have the same rights and chances.
examples: They share the housework in a very *egalitarian* way.
The company has an *egalitarian* culture with no private offices.
The Nordic countries are among the *most egalitarian* in the world.

senses.gloss: Thinking only about yourself and not about other people.
examples: Toddlers are naturally *egocentric*.
He's an *egocentric* boss who never listens.
She became *more egocentric* after she got famous.

contrast: *egotistical* means 'thinking you are very important and talking about yourself'; *selfish* means 'caring only about your own needs'. Russian *эгоистичный* is usually *selfish*.

senses.gloss: Thinking you are better or more important than other people.
examples: He's so *egotistical* that he only talks about himself.
The *egotistical* star refused to share the stage.
She's the *most egotistical* person I've ever worked with.

senses.gloss: Extremely bad and very obvious.
examples: It was an *egregious* error by the referee.
The company was fined for *egregious* safety violations.
This is the *most egregious* case of fraud the court has seen.

senses.gloss: Of or from Egypt, ancient or modern, its people or its culture.
examples: The museum has a large collection of ancient *Egyptian* art.
My doctor is *Egyptian*.
*Egyptian* cotton sheets are soft and expensive.

contrast: The adjective ends in /ərət/; the verb *to elaborate* (give more details) ends in /əreɪt/: *Can you ih-LAB-uh-rayt?*

senses.gloss: Having many carefully planned parts or details.
examples: They planned an *elaborate* surprise party.
The dress had *elaborate* embroidery on the sleeves.
Each year the holiday decorations get *more elaborate*.

contrast: *elastic* is also a noun, the stretchy material: *The elastic in these shorts is worn out*.

senses.gloss: Able to stretch and then go back to its original shape.
examples: The pants have an *elastic* waistband.
Skin becomes less *elastic* with age.
This fabric is *more elastic* than cotton.

senses.gloss: Able to change or be changed easily.
examples: "Soon" is a very *elastic* word in this office.
Demand for gasoline is not very *elastic*.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *We were elated*

senses.gloss: Extremely happy and excited.
examples: She was *elated* at the news of her promotion.
The *elated* fans ran onto the field.
I've never seen him *more elated* than on the day his son was born.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the passive: *She was elected mayor*
contrast: A person who has won but not yet started the job is *-elect*, after the noun: *the president-elect*, *the governor-elect*.

senses.gloss: Chosen by voting.
examples: *Elected* officials should listen to voters.
The city has an *elected* school board.
She was the first *elected* female governor of the state.

contrast: In American schools *an elective* is a noun, 'an optional class': *I'm taking photography as an elective*.

senses.gloss: Chosen, not required; of medical treatment, planned rather than urgent.
examples: Hospitals postponed all *elective* surgery.
Art is an *elective* course at our high school.
Many insurers don't cover *elective* procedures.

senses.gloss: Relating to an election or filled by an election.
examples: She has never held *elective* office.
The governor is the highest *elective* position in the state.

senses.gloss: Relating to elections or voting.
examples: The candidate needs 270 votes in the *Electoral* College.
Some states are changing their *electoral* maps.
There was no evidence of *electoral* fraud.

senses.gloss: Very exciting.
examples: The band gave an *electrifying* performance.
The atmosphere in the stadium was *electrifying*.
It was the *most electrifying* finish in years.

senses.gloss: Relating to electricity and magnetism together.
examples: Light is a form of *electromagnetic* radiation.
The device creates a strong *electromagnetic* field.
Radio waves are part of the *electromagnetic* spectrum.

contrast: *electronic* devices use microchips and circuits (a phone, a computer); *electric* things simply run on electricity (*an electric fan*, *an electric car*); *electrical* describes the system or work (*electrical wiring*, *an electrical engineer*).

senses.gloss: Using microchips, transistors or other parts that control electric current.
examples: Please turn off all *electronic* devices during takeoff.
The store sells *electronic* equipment and appliances.

senses.gloss: Done, sent or stored using computers.
examples: We accept *electronic* payments only.
Doctors now keep *electronic* medical records.
The music is fully *electronic*, with no live instruments.

senses.gloss: Graceful, attractive and stylish.
examples: She wore an *elegant* black dress.
The hotel lobby is simple but *elegant*.
The new design is *more elegant* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Of an idea or solution: clever and simple.
examples: It's an *elegant* solution to a difficult problem.
The proof is short and *elegant*.

position: both — the chemistry sense only before a noun: *elemental carbon*
contrast: Not the same as *elementary* (basic, simple): *an elementary mistake*, but *elemental forces of nature*.

senses.gloss: Basic and powerful, like the forces of nature.
examples: The storm showed the *elemental* power of the sea.
Fear of the dark is one of the *most elemental* human fears.

senses.gloss: In chemistry: in the form of a pure chemical element.
examples: Diamonds are made of *elemental* carbon.
*Elemental* sodium reacts violently with water.

position: both — the school sense only before a noun: *elementary school*
comparison: more/most — *more elementary*, *most elementary*, in the 'basic' sense

senses.gloss: Basic and simple.
examples: He made an *elementary* mistake in the math.
The questions were fairly *elementary*.
Let's start with the *most elementary* rules of grammar.

senses.gloss: Relating to the first stage of school, for children aged about 5 to 11.
examples: My daughter is in *elementary* school.
He's been an *elementary* teacher for twenty years.

senses.gloss: Higher than normal in level or amount.
examples: The test showed *elevated* levels of lead in the water.
Her blood pressure was slightly *elevated*.

senses.gloss: Raised above the ground.
examples: Chicago's *elevated* trains are called the L.
The house sits on an *elevated* site above the river.

senses.gloss: Formal, serious or high in rank or style.
examples: The speech was written in *elevated* language.
Her tone became *more elevated* when the cameras were on.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an elite school*
contrast: *the elite* is a noun, the most powerful or talented group. *elitist* is the disapproving word for a person or attitude that looks down on ordinary people.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the best, most skilled or most powerful group.
examples: She trained with *elite* athletes before the Olympics.
He was a member of an *elite* military unit.
It's one of the *most elite* colleges in the country.

contrast: It refers to Queen Elizabeth I (1558–1603), the age of Shakespeare, not to Elizabeth II.

senses.gloss: From the time of Queen Elizabeth I of England, or in its style.
examples: We're studying *Elizabethan* drama this semester.
The actors wore *Elizabethan* costumes.
The manor house is *Elizabethan*, built in 1580.
